extracted.intended_audience: educated general readership interested in history, biography, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for judging historical figures and composing critical biographical essays — how to weigh context, motive, public perception, and evidence when assessing a statesman or public person. Emphasises balancing intellectual achievements with public actions and legal/ethical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge across ages without context
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought not to try the men of one age by the standard of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider contemporary customs and mores before condemning historical actors; temper modern moral indignation with understanding of period norms. However, this rule is not absolute — some practices were already condemned in their own time and thus cannot be excused by 'different age' arguments (for example, torturing prisoners was widely regarded as barbarous and illegal in Bacon's time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish speculation from action
rubrics_metrics.description: Those only judge of him correctly who take in at one view Bacon in speculation and Bacon in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the subject's intellectual/philosophical achievements (library, studies, contributions to learning) and their public, political, or judicial conduct; one side may be laudable while the other shameful, and a full judgment must incorporate both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether conduct conformed to established practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Was he conforming to an usage then generally admitted to be proper? ... He was not even the last lingering adherent of an old abuse. He was guilty of attempting to introduce into the courts of law an odious abuse for which no precedent could be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or condemning an action, check for contemporaneous precedents and authoritative statements (e.g., Coke's protest). If no precedent exists and contemporaries regard it as novel, citing custom as excuse is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary legal and moral standards as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of torturing prisoners was then generally acknowledged by lawyers to be illegal, and was execrated by the public as barbarous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on documented legal decisions, public opinion, and official orders of the period (e.g., royal prohibitions, earlier apologies) to judge whether an act was accepted or condemned at the time; do not assume that an abuse was lawful merely because later historians debate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge officials by duties of office and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge who listens to private solicitations is a disgrace to his post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate office-holders by whether they upheld the plainest rules of duty (impartiality, refusing to be influenced by favourites, refraining from private interference in pending causes). Expressed admonitions by the subject (e.g., advising others against interference) should be weighed against their actual conduct in office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh motive and ambition against public duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who survey only one-half of his character may speak of him with unmixed admiration or with unmixed contempt. ... The difference between Bacon the philosopher and Bacon the Attorney‑General, Bacon seeking for truth, and Bacon seeking for the Seals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether actions arose from honest intellectual aims or from unworthy ambition and self‑interest; consider how ambition may explain, but not excuse, departures from integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate consequences and abuse of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all patents in our history, the most disgraceful was that which was granted to Sir Giles Mompesson... The patentees were armed with powers as great as have ever been given to farmers of the revenue... These formidable powers were used for purposes viler than even those for which they were given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the practical outcomes of a subject's decisions (economic harm, oppression, corruption), particularly when public office was used to enrich favourites or to enforce monopolies; tangible harms strengthen condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish personal charm from moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: His talents secured him from contempt, his temper and his manners from hatred... a man of great abilities, whose abilities are united with caution, good humour, patience, and affability... had power to reconcile him to those whom he had most offended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that wit, charm, and social graces can mask serious faults and cause contemporaries to overlook misconduct; explicit attention should be paid to whether public esteem derives from character or mere polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider differing standards for contemporaries vs posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the qualities which make a man an object of interest and veneration to posterity, they cannot be compared together. But in the qualities by which chiefly a man is known to his contemporaries there was a striking similarity between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about historical figures, separate the traits that win immediate social favor from those that secure long-term reputation; explain why posterity may judge differently and on what bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand rigorous use of evidence and precedent in defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither Bacon nor Mr. Montagu has shown a single precedent... Coke... asserted it to be new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defender of controversial acts must produce concrete precedents or authoritative corroboration; absence of such evidence undermines claims that conduct was customary or acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute different moral responsibility by role and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who intrust a petulant, hot-blooded, ill-informed lad with power, are more to blame than he for the mischief which he may do with it... Bacon was the ablest public man then living in Europe. He was near sixty years old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the subject's age, experience, and station: youthful ignorance is more forgivable than the misconduct of a seasoned, knowledgeable statesman who should have known better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how exceptional ability can enable enormous harm
rubrics_metrics.description: History were not made up of the bad actions of extraordinary men... nine-tenths of the calamities which have befallen the human race had any other origin than the union of high intelligence with low desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing culpability, note that great talents amplify the impact of immoral choices; moral appraisal should factor in how intellect and ambition combined to produce public damage.
